title: Metamodernism
thinkers: David Foster Wallace (forerunner of the "New Sincerity")
keyWorks: D. F. Wallace, "E Unibus Pluram: Television and U.S. Fiction" (1993)
T. Vermeulen, R. van den Akker, "Notes on Metamodernism" (2010)
Metamodernism: Historicity, Affect, and Depth after Postmodernism (edited volume, 2017)
summary: Metamodernism is a concept proposed in 2010 by the Dutch cultural theorists Timotheus Vermeulen and Robin van den Akker to describe the "structure of feeling" of our time. It is not a philosophical school in the strict sense but a way of understanding how, after postmodern irony, people are once again daring to be sincere, to hope, and to reach for big meanings — without forgetting their doubts. Metamodernism's central image is oscillation: a swinging back and forth between opposites.
onEmotions: For metamodernism, feelings are not something to be embarrassed about or to hide behind irony. A "structure of feeling" (a phrase coined by the cultural critic Raymond Williams) is the shared emotional climate of an era, and today, Vermeulen and van den Akker suggest, it oscillates between enthusiasm and skepticism, hope and melancholy. The metamodern person can know that their feelings are "naive" and still live them seriously — this is called "informed naivety." Contradictory feelings here are not a mistake but a normal state: you can laugh and cry at once, believe and doubt at once.

anxiety.text: "We must go forth and oscillate!" — so ends Luke Turner's Metamodernist Manifesto. If you are pulled in different directions at once and it makes you anxious, you are not alone. Metamodernism describes this state as a feature of our era: Vermeulen and van den Akker speak of "oscillation" — a swinging between opposite poles, such as hope and doubt, engagement and detachment. In their view, this swinging need not be forcibly stopped by choosing one side forever. They use the Greek word "metaxy" — "in-betweenness," the state of being "between." Seen this way, anxiety is not a breakdown but a sign that you are living in the tension between two things that matter to you. You might try not to win this inner argument right away, but to sway between the poles like a pendulum — and notice a kind of steadiness in motion too.
anxiety.practice: Stand up and slowly shift your weight from one foot to the other, like a pendulum, silently naming the two poles you are swinging between. After a minute, notice: there is steadiness in motion too.

fear.text: "As if" — Vermeulen and van den Akker made this formula of Kant's one of the keys to metamodernism: act as if the goal were achievable, even knowing there are no guarantees. The fear of taking a step that might not work out is familiar to anyone who tries something in earnest. They describe this as a movement that does not wait for certainty of success. This is not recklessness, nor a naive belief that all will be well. It is "informed naivety": you understand the risks, you can see it might not work out — and you still choose to try, because the path itself has meaning. Fear does not have to be fully conquered before you move. It can walk beside you, like a sober companion, while you take a small step "as if."
fear.practice: Take one small step "as if" everything were going to work out: send the email, dial the number, open the door. Promise no result — only the step.

quote.text: Metamodernism moves for the sake of moving, attempts in spite of its inevitable failure; it seeks forever for a truth that it never expects to find.
quote.author: Timotheus Vermeulen, Robin van den Akker

sadness.text: A childlike, almost naive brightness beside a quiet sorrow — scholars of metamodernism find this combination in Wes Anderson's films and in countless songs of recent years. Sadness doesn't need to justify itself. Metamodernism seems to understand it especially well: Vermeulen and van den Akker name melancholy as one of the poles between which the feeling of our time oscillates — alongside hope. Postmodernism often hid sadness behind irony — "oh well, none of this is serious." The metamodern sensibility allows you to be sad in earnest without losing your capacity for lightness. Sadness is not the opposite of hope but its neighbor. You can let it be, knowing the pendulum will swing the other way too — not because you force it, but because that is how a living feeling works.
sadness.practice: Put on a film scene or a song where sadness and tenderness sound together, and stay with it to the end without switching. Metamodernism is all about this "sad, but warm."

grief.text: Metamodernism grew in large part out of weariness with postmodern detachment, when it was customary to speak of the most important things with a smirk. Grief is a feeling with no room for irony, and rightly so. Loss breaks through that defense: in the face of it, you cannot "pretend." Grief brings us back to the "New Sincerity" — a readiness to speak plainly and feel in earnest, even if it looks vulnerable. At the same time, metamodernism does not ask you to choose a single state: in grief, tears can sit beside unexpected laughter over a shared memory, pain beside gratitude. This swinging is not a betrayal of the loss. It is a sign that you are alive and that you love, and you can accept it without judgment.
grief.practice: Tell someone one funny story about the person or thing you have lost — the kind that hurts and makes you smile at once. Metamodernism lets tears and laughter sit side by side.

loneliness.text: Irony is good for exposing things but nearly useless for building anything — so thought David Foster Wallace, a forerunner of the "New Sincerity." Loneliness can feel especially sharp in a world where everyone seems to be constantly connected. Metamodernism describes an era grown tired of ironic watching from the sidelines. It is hard to truly meet someone from behind irony. Part of loneliness may come from a habit of keeping your distance, of always being "a little above" your own feelings. The metamodern answer is "informed naivety": risking saying plainly "I'm lonely" or "I miss you," knowing it may sound awkward. Sincerity is vulnerable, but it is exactly what opens the door through which another person can come in.
loneliness.practice: Call or message one person for no reason and with no joke at the end: "I miss you" or "I've been thinking of you." This is a small act of the "New Sincerity."

anger.text: "Pragmatic idealism" is what Vermeulen and van den Akker call the wish to change something together with a sober understanding that the result will not be ideal. Anger can be an honest response to something that matters to you. Postmodern culture often taught us to meet injustice with an ironic shrug: "well, that's how the world is." Metamodernism describes a return of seriousness. Anger is not something to mock or hide. It can become the energy of idealism. But metamodernism also offers oscillation: between hot engagement and a step back, between conviction and doubt about being right. You can let your anger sound at full strength and still leave a small window open inside for the question: "What if I'm not seeing everything?"
anger.practice: Say aloud what makes you angry — at full strength — and then add one sentence that begins with "And yet, perhaps…". That is what oscillation sounds like.

shame.text: In 1993 David Foster Wallace predicted that the new rebels would be those who dared to step back from irony and seriously stand up for simple values, at the risk of looking sentimental. Shame is often tied to exactly this fear of seeming ridiculous, naive, "too much." Postmodernism made irony the main defense: if you say everything with a smirk, no one can catch you having a sincere feeling. Metamodernism describes a turn in which this defense stops working and starts to feel cramped. Shame about "too strong" feelings is largely an echo of a cultural norm, not the truth about you. You might try "informed naivety": admit that you know how it looks from outside — and still stay with your feeling.
shame.practice: Name one feeling or passion you are embarrassed about as "naive." Say to yourself: "Yes, it's naive — and it's mine."

quote.text: The next real literary "rebels" in this country might well emerge as some weird bunch of anti-rebels, born oglers who dare somehow to back away from ironic watching, who have the childish gall actually to endorse and instantiate single-entendre principles.
quote.author: David Foster Wallace
quote.source: "E Unibus Pluram: Television and U.S. Fiction" (1993)

guilt.text: "Everyone lives like this," "nothing matters" — postmodern culture sometimes taught us to dissolve guilt with irony. Guilt is a sign that your actions and other people matter to you. Metamodernism doesn't write about guilt directly, but its ideas suggest another path. The metamodern sensibility gives actions their weight back — while remembering imperfection. "Pragmatic idealism" means striving to act well while knowing in advance that you won't be perfect. In this light, guilt is not proof that you are a bad person but a moment of oscillation between the ideal and reality. You can acknowledge a mistake seriously, do what is within your power, and then let the pendulum swing back — toward accepting yourself as imperfect but trying.
guilt.practice: Take one small repairing action — apologize, give something back, finish what you left undone — and then tell yourself: "I'm imperfect, and I'm trying." This is what pragmatic idealism looks like.

envy.text: Pretending you "don't care," that you're above it — this is how postmodern culture often taught us to hide our desires. Envy is unpleasant, but it honestly shows you what you want. If we follow this thought, envy is a desire that was denied the right to sincerity. Metamodernism offers the "New Sincerity": admit your desire plainly, without the self-irony that devalues it. And at the same time stay clear-eyed, remembering that you only see part of someone else's life. This swinging between "I really want this" and "I don't know the whole picture" makes envy less corrosive. It becomes a hint: what you truly value — and what small step toward it is possible without comparison.
envy.practice: Say aloud, sincerely and without irony: "I want…" — and finish the sentence. Notice what you felt.

emptiness.text: "Reconstruction" instead of endless deconstruction — this is how Vermeulen and van den Akker describe a new generation's answer to the emptiness left after postmodernism. When nothing touches you and you feel empty inside, it is hard. Metamodernism grew in large part out of an awareness of this kind of emptiness at the end of the 20th century. Postmodernism taught culture to see that any big meaning could be taken apart, exposed and mocked — and many people felt that nothing was left underneath. It is not a return to naive faith but an attempt to build meaning anew, while understanding that there may be no final answer. Emptiness is not the last word about the world but a pause between meanings taken apart and meanings not yet put together. You don't have to rush it, but you can leave the door ajar.
emptiness.practice: Stage a small "reconstruction": put three things side by side that were once dear to you — a photo, a book, a mug — and see which of them still speaks to you.

confusion.text: Believing and doubting, building and dismantling at once — this, for Vermeulen and van den Akker, is how the culture of our time thinks. Confusion is a natural reaction to a time with no single shared answer. Metamodernism describes an era in which the old grand narratives of progress have weakened, while pure irony has also stopped comforting us. Vermeulen and van den Akker propose accepting this state not as chaos but as oscillation — a swinging between opposites that never comes to a final stop. Confusion is not a sign that you've missed something but an honest reflection of the era. You can allow yourself not to make a final choice yet, and keep moving even as you waver.
confusion.practice: Walk for a few minutes and with each step alternate in your mind: "on the one hand…", "on the other hand…". Don't close it off — let both sides be true for now.

quote.text: Metamodernism oscillates between a modern enthusiasm and a postmodern irony, between hope and melancholy, between naïveté and knowingness, empathy and apathy, unity and plurality, totality and fragmentation, purity and ambiguity.
quote.author: Timotheus Vermeulen, Robin van den Akker

fatigue.text: Irony that becomes the norm turns from liberation into tyranny — so thought David Foster Wallace. Fatigue can come from work, and it can also come from constantly having to stay on the defensive. Metamodernism helps you notice a particular fatigue of our time — fatigue from irony. When everything has to be devalued with a joke, when nothing can be loved openly and nothing invested in seriously, it takes enormous hidden effort. Metamodernism suggests not trading irony for heroic enthusiasm — that is exhausting too — but allowing yourself to swing between engagement and rest. A pendulum has a moment when it pauses at the far end of its arc. Your fatigue may be that moment — not a defeat, but a natural part of the motion.
fatigue.practice: Find one area where you're tired of "keeping a straight face," and stop for five minutes: sit however is comfortable, sigh out loud, make no jokes.

boredom.text: "Romanticize the world," Novalis urged: give the ordinary a mysterious aspect, the familiar the dignity of the unknown. Boredom can seem like a sign that the world is used up and everything has been done before. This is a very postmodern feeling: everything is a quotation, everything a repeat. Metamodernism answers it with a turn toward what Vermeulen and van den Akker call neo-romanticism. This is not denying that the world is full of repetition, but a conscious decision to look at the familiar as if something greater were hidden in it — that very "informed naivety." Boredom, then, is an invitation to a small experiment: to treat a familiar thing seriously and with wonder, even while knowing it's a bit of a game.
boredom.practice: Walk a familiar route as if you were in an unknown fairy-tale town: look for the "magical" — an odd sign, light in a window, a crooked tree. Novalis would call this romanticizing.

quote.text: The world must be romanticized. […] Insofar as I present the commonplace with higher meaning, the customary with a mysterious appearance, the known with the dignity of the unknown, the finite with an infinite appearance, I romanticize it.
quote.author: Novalis

joy.text: Delight seemed naive, enthusiasm a little ridiculous: postmodern culture often regarded open joy with suspicion. Metamodernism rehabilitates joy, and yours needs no justification. Metamodernism describes the return of what Vermeulen and van den Akker call modern enthusiasm — but now without the illusion that happiness will be eternal and unclouded. This is joy with open eyes: you know about the world's troubles and still allow yourself to rejoice. Such "informed naivety" is not foolish but brave. Joy doesn't need to be justified or devalued with a joke — you can simply live it. And if the pendulum later swings toward sadness, that won't cancel the fact that the joy was real.
joy.practice: Put on one song and move to it as if no one were watching — in earnest and a little ridiculous at the same time. That is "informed naivety," only in the body.

love.text: Postmodern irony taught us to say a plain "I love you" in quotation marks — as if it were a cliché too awkward to utter. The tenderness you feel is the main territory of the "New Sincerity." Metamodernism describes a culture that once again dares to use that cliché, knowing it is a cliché — and says it in earnest anyway. That is "informed naivety": remembering the whole history of words about love and choosing them all the same. Tenderness doesn't need originality. It can be expressed through simple, even banal gestures — and they will be real because you put yourself into them. To love in the metamodern sense is to risk looking sentimental for the sake of genuine closeness.
love.practice: Say the simplest, most "banal" phrase of tenderness to someone you love — in earnest, looking them in the eye or over the phone.

gratitude.text: A "thank you" said in earnest is one of the purest forms of the "New Sincerity." The gratitude you feel admits that you depend on others, and that there's nothing wrong with that. Postmodern culture was often embarrassed by such simplicity. Thanking someone without a joke seemed naive, almost awkward. The metamodern sensibility, as Vermeulen and van den Akker describe it, reaches toward restoring meaning where it has been taken apart — toward "reconstruction" instead of endless deconstruction. Gratitude is just such a small reconstruction: out of scattered events, you assemble a coherent story of what you have been given. You can allow yourself to give thanks directly, without self-irony, even if it seems a little old-fashioned. A simple "thank you" is often the most precise word.
gratitude.practice: Thank one person directly, without self-irony: name exactly what they gave you and when. Let it sound a little old-fashioned.

hope.text: Kant's "as if" lies at the heart of metamodern hope: acting as though the world could move toward the better, though there is no proof. Your hope may be exactly like that — and it isn't naive. This is neither the naive optimism of modernity, which believed in inevitable progress, nor postmodern skepticism, which declared all hope an illusion. It is a hope that knows its own fragility and chooses to exist anyway. Vermeulen and van den Akker speak of hope and melancholy as two poles of a single movement. You can hope without promising yourself a result and without being ashamed of your doubts. Hope here is not a forecast but a way of keeping your direction as you walk.
hope.practice: Today, do one small thing as if what you hope for were already beginning to come true: plant a seed, clear a shelf, make a call.

nostalgia.text: Vintage things, film photography, remakes of old stories — scholars of metamodernism note that the culture of recent years is full of longing for the past. Your nostalgia is one of the most characteristic feelings of our time, and there is nothing shameful in it. Postmodernism treated the past as a set of quotations for ironic play. The metamodern attitude is different: the past once again becomes a source of sincere feeling, even though we know it cannot be brought back and that it was not ideal. This is nostalgia with open eyes — a swinging between tenderness for what is gone and a sober understanding of its limits. You can allow yourself to miss the past without turning it into a myth and without being ashamed of your attachment.
nostalgia.practice: Take out one object or photo from that time and hold it in your hands. Tell yourself: "It wasn't perfect — and still, what's dear to me is…"

craving.text: "Morning, boys. How's the water?" — "What the hell is water?" With this joke about fish, David Foster Wallace, a forerunner of the "New Sincerity," opens his speech "This Is Water." A sharp craving — "I want it right now" — can be very strong, and there's nothing shameful in that. In that speech Wallace talks about our "default setting" — automatic reactions that switch on by themselves, like water you don't notice. His thought is that real freedom is not the absence of desires but the ability, at least sometimes, to choose what to pay attention to. A craving is a default setting announcing itself loudly. You don't need to defeat it once and for all. You can simply notice: "there it is" — and with that small noticing, already step a little out of autopilot.
craving.practice: When a craving rises, say to yourself: "This is the default setting." Then shift your attention to one thing near you — a sound, your breath, the feeling in your palms — for at least a minute.

addiction.text: David Foster Wallace's Infinite Jest is in large part about addiction and about people trying to get free of it. Addiction is not a moral failure but a circle that is genuinely hard to get out of. Wallace portrays mutual-help groups with great respect: their simple slogans like "one day at a time" seem banal to the ironic mind, but, as the characters notice, they somehow work if you say them in earnest. This is a very metamodern thought: you don't have to fully believe or understand everything in order to try sincerely. Getting out of the circle, then, is not a heroic leap but a willingness to do simple things again and again, irony set aside, together with others.
addiction.practice: Choose one simple phrase of support that seems a little banal to you and say it to yourself today in earnest. If you like, you could drop in on a mutual-help group such as AA or NA — just to listen.

hangover.text: Yesterday everything was easy and a little ironic, today it's serious and heavy: metamodernism would call this a sharp swing of the pendulum. The morning after can be hard: your body aches, anxiety, shame and gaps in memory come too — and none of this makes you any worse a person. Metamodernism describes such swings as the ordinary rhythm of our time, not as a breakdown. It suggests not choosing one extreme — neither "no big deal, forget it" nor "I'm a terrible person." You can hold both sides: yes, it was fun, and yes, right now it's bad. "Informed naivety" lets you honestly acknowledge what happened and still treat yourself with warmth rather than a verdict.
hangover.practice: Drink a glass of water and tell yourself two sentences, both in earnest: "Yesterday was what it was" and "Today I'll take care of myself."

euphoria.text: Vermeulen and van den Akker name enthusiasm as one of the poles between which the feeling of our time oscillates. Euphoria, when everything seems possible, doesn't need to be spoiled with skepticism. After a long era of postmodern irony, when delight seemed naive, metamodernism rehabilitates it: you can rejoice in earnest. At the same time, the metamodern person knows the pendulum swings, and the high will give way to something else. This knowledge doesn't cancel the joy but makes it gentler. You can fully live the euphoria while remembering that it is one phase of the oscillation, not a new permanent world. And when the wave settles, what may remain is the memory that the world is capable of being this open.
euphoria.practice: Describe in two or three words what exactly is bringing you joy right now, and keep the note for another phase of the pendulum — later it will remind you that such a feeling is possible.

crash.text: The pendulum is metamodernism's central image: feeling swings between enthusiasm and melancholy, hope and doubt. The drop after a high can be very hard — as if the world had suddenly faded — and it is not your fault. The comedown is not proof that the high was unreal, but the pendulum swinging the other way. Metamodernism does not treat melancholy as a mistake: it is just as legitimate a pole as joy. The main thing is to remember that the pendulum doesn't get stuck forever. Even if right now it seems otherwise. Right now you don't have to demand that the brightness come back; you can simply live in this phase, knowing it will pass too. A pendulum swings precisely in order to come back.
crash.practice: Hang a key or a ring on a thread, give it a swing, and watch until the pendulum settles by itself. Don't hurry it — just watch.

quote.text: We must go forth and oscillate!
quote.author: Luke Turner

panic.text: The oscillation metamodernism speaks of works like a wave: it rises and, sooner or later, falls. Panic is very frightening: a wave of terror, as if your heart and breathing had stopped obeying you. You are not alone in this, and such a wave usually peaks and subsides within a few minutes. Only one thing matters: to ride it out, holding on to something simple. Right now there's no need to analyze or understand anything — neither ironically nor seriously. Metamodernism values the simple and direct, and in a moment of panic the most direct thing is the body: the floor under your feet, your breath, the objects around you. You can come back to thinking later, once the wave has passed.
panic.practice: Rock gently back and forth, standing or sitting, like a pendulum, and with each swing make the exhale longer than the inhale. Name aloud five objects around you, one after another.

dread.text: Living "as if" the world had meaning and direction, while knowing there is no proof — this is how Vermeulen and van den Akker describe the metamodern attitude to the big questions. The question "what's the point of it all," the sense of an abyss, is one of the heaviest feelings, and there is a lot of honesty in it. This is not self-deception but a conscious choice to live in earnest. Meaning here is not found ready-made but built — day by day, together with others. Metamodernism does not abolish the abyss, but it doesn't fall into it either: it oscillates between doubt and hope and keeps building meaning. The answer to "what's the point" is not final — it is the one you choose to live out today.
dread.practice: Give one minute today to one thing you're willing to live for "as if" it had meaning — a person, a cause, something beautiful. Do something very small for it.

fomo.text: Sehnsucht is what the German Romantics called the yearning for something greater, better, far away, and Vermeulen and van den Akker find "neo-romantic" features in our culture. The feeling that everyone else is living more interesting lives and you're not where you should be is very familiar to our time. The fear of missing out is romantic longing in the age of the feed. The feed simply gives it endless occasions. Metamodernism doesn't ask you to get rid of it, but offers oscillation: acknowledge the pull toward "there" and at the same time notice the value of "here." You can want something else without devaluing your own life. "There" will always look brighter, because it is a picture, while "here" is life.
fomo.practice: Step out for five minutes right where you are — into the yard, onto the balcony — and find one thing that appears in no feed. "Out there" can wait.

sleepless.text: "Structure of feeling" is Raymond Williams's phrase, which metamodernists use for the shared emotional climate of an era. Lying awake at three in the morning is exhausting, and it is not your fault. At night the protective irony of the day usually weakens, and thoughts become bare and heavy. And you share this climate with many people: you are not the only one lying awake thinking about life right now. Metamodernism doesn't require you to resolve every question in order to fall asleep. It accepts that some questions can be held open, swinging between anxiety and hope. The night doesn't owe you answers. You can put the search for meaning off until morning and simply let yourself lie there.
sleepless.practice: Lying down, feel the weight of your body on the bed and take a few slow exhales. With each one, silently set aside one question with the words "I'll come back to this in the morning."

betrayal.text: "Informed naivety" is a key idea of metamodernism: knowing people can let you down and still not giving up your capacity to trust. Betrayal wounds deeply, and that pain is legitimate: you trusted, and your trust was deceived. After something like this it's easy to decide that sincerity is naivety and to hide behind cynicism. Metamodernism knows this crossroads well: postmodern irony was, in large part, exactly that kind of defense. The "New Sincerity" suggests not choosing once and for all between trust and cynicism. Your trust wasn't foolishness, it was courage. Betrayal speaks about another person's action, not about openness having been a mistake. You can acknowledge the pain fully without concluding that you can never trust anyone again.
betrayal.practice: Write: "I don't want to lose my capacity for…" — and finish the sentence. That is what's worth protecting no matter what.

jealousy.text: "I don't care," "I'm above it" — this is how postmodern culture taught us to hide jealousy behind irony. But jealousy is agonizing, and often behind it lies the fear of losing someone very dear. Metamodernism suggests being more honest: acknowledge the jealousy without being ashamed of it and without letting it take control. Through metamodern eyes, jealousy is an oscillation between love and fear, trust and doubt. Both poles are real. Love and fear each tell their own truth here. You don't have to choose between "I simply love" and "I'm simply afraid" — you can acknowledge both. A sincere "I'm scared of losing you" is often closer to the truth than control or coldness.
jealousy.practice: If the moment is right, say one sentence to the person you love, without irony or reproach: "I'm scared of losing you." Ask for nothing more.

resentment.text: Against endless deconstruction — taking apart, exposing, looking for the catch — Vermeulen and van den Akker set "reconstruction": an attempt to build something anew. Old resentment is heavy — you really were hurt. Metamodernists don't write about resentment, but it often resembles an endless deconstruction of a single situation: it gets taken apart again and again, turning up ever new evidence of injustice. Metamodernism doesn't demand that you forget or forgive. It only suggests that, alongside taking the past apart, you try to build something new — however small, however uncertain. The resentment can remain part of your story, but it doesn't have to be its only plot. Beside it, another plot can appear — about what you are building now.
resentment.practice: Build something small with your own hands today — arrange some flowers, fix a thing, cook a simple dish. Reconstruction starts small and can have nothing to do with the resentment.

heartbreak.text: In Michel Gondry's Eternal Sunshine of the Spotless Mind — a film often cited as an example of the metamodern sensibility — two people erase their memories of each other, yet in the end decide to try again, even though they already know it may hurt. When your heart is broken it hurts almost physically, and that pain speaks of how much you invested. Metamodernism treats love without quotation marks. That is "informed naivety": knowing the risk and still choosing openness. Your pain is not proof that loving was foolish. It is part of what makes love real, and it doesn't cancel your ability to love again.
heartbreak.practice: Choose one memory of this relationship you wouldn't erase, and stay with it for a minute with your eyes closed, even if it hurts.

impostor.text: "In spite of inevitable failure" — this is how Vermeulen and van den Akker describe the metamodern movement: trying in earnest, knowing there will be no perfection. The fear of being found out at any moment is familiar to a great many people — even to those you admire. Feeling like an impostor is a sign that you have taken something on seriously rather than hiding behind the irony of "I wasn't even trying." No one is ever fully "ready." The metamodern person admits to being a little naive and does it anyway. Even those you admire started out unsure. Your doubt doesn't cancel your work. You can doubt and keep going at the same time — metamodernism considers exactly that kind of oscillation natural.
impostor.practice: Tell someone what you have taken on seriously despite your doubts, and what you have already done. Don't play it down.

self_hatred.text: "Irony... is the voice of the trapped who have come to enjoy their cage" — Wallace quotes this line of Lewis Hyde's in "E Unibus Pluram." The inner critic can sound very convincing, but its verdict is not the truth about you. David Foster Wallace, a forerunner of the "New Sincerity," wrote about how irony, which at first helped expose lies, over time becomes a trap: it devalues everything, including ourselves. The inner critic often speaks in the very language of this merciless irony: it mocks, devalues, leaves nothing alive. Metamodernism suggests stepping back from that voice and allowing yourself sincerity toward yourself — saying something warm about yourself, even if it seems naive. Such kindness to yourself is not self-deception but a refusal to live in a cage of constant mockery.
self_hatred.practice: Write down one mocking phrase from your inner critic. Then, next to it, write one sincere, warm sentence about yourself, even if it seems naive.

quote.text: Irony has only emergency use. Carried over time, it is the voice of the trapped who have come to enjoy their cage.
quote.author: Lewis Hyde (quoted by David Foster Wallace)
quote.source: D. F. Wallace, "E Unibus Pluram: Television and U.S. Fiction" (1993)

helplessness.text: Acting as if the world could become better, even without guarantees — this is what Vermeulen and van den Akker call "pragmatic idealism." Feeling powerless to change anything is hard, and it often reflects real circumstances rather than any weakness of yours. Metamodernism knows this feeling well: our time is full of huge problems in the face of which a single person seems small. Helplessness and hope don't exclude each other — you can swing between them. You don't have to believe in success in order to take a small step. Sometimes it is the step that brings back a little faith, not the other way round. It's enough to act "as if." A small step taken in earnest is no longer helplessness but participation.
helplessness.practice: Choose one tiny thing that is within your power today, and do it "as if" it mattered.

procrastination.text: "As long as I haven't started, no one can say I failed" — this is the ironic defense metamodernism helps you spot in putting things off. When you can't get started, it is more often fear, fatigue, or the sense that everything has to be done perfectly than laziness. Vermeulen and van den Akker describe the metamodern movement as an attempt made "in spite of inevitable failure." This means you can begin while accepting imperfection in advance. Metamodernism doesn't require confidence; it offers "informed naivety": knowing it will be hard and still taking the first small step. An imperfect beginning is better than a perfect plan that stays in your head — and it says nothing about your worth.
procrastination.practice: Do the smallest part of the task — one sentence, one email — deliberately imperfectly, "in spite of inevitable failure." Note that you have started.

uprooted.text: Vermeulen and van den Akker link the word "meta" to Plato's "metaxy" — "between." Being cut off from home — a move, emigration, losing familiar ground — is a real loss, and there is no need to play down its weight. The metamodern person lives between poles: between past and future, irony and sincerity. Living between two places, two languages, two cultures is not a failure or a flaw but a particular way of being. You can long for your old home and build a new one at the same time, without choosing one. Metamodernism doesn't require you to decide where you "really" are. You can be "in between" and find your own truth in that. Many people today live exactly like this — in between — and find in it not only loss but richness.
uprooted.practice: Stand in a doorway for a minute — one foot in one room, the other in the next. Feel that you can stand steadily "in between" too.

overload.text: Screen culture draws us in, and ironic watching from the sidelines becomes a habit — David Foster Wallace wrote this back in his 1993 essay on television. If the feed and the noise have worn you out, that is a response to your environment, not a weakness of yours. And in his speech "This Is Water" he said that what matters most is learning to choose what to pay attention to amid the endless stream. The feed is the water we swim in and hardly notice. Simply noticing it is already a first step toward freedom. You don't need to give up everything; you can choose a few things. Two or three things chosen deliberately give more than a hundred scrolled past.
overload.practice: Close the feed for two minutes and ask yourself: "What do I actually want to pay attention to right now?" — and then turn your attention there.

quote.text: The really important kind of freedom involves attention and awareness and discipline, and being able truly to care about other people and to sacrifice for them over and over in myriad petty, unsexy ways every day.
quote.author: David Foster Wallace

unreality.text: A world of simulations and copies, where it is hard to find anything "real," is postmodernism's central theme. The feeling that nothing is quite real can be unsettling, and it deserves gentle care. Metamodernism, as Vermeulen and van den Akker see it, responds with a renewed interest in depth, authenticity and the real — even while understanding that we can never finally arrive at them. In the age of screens, the sense of unreality visits many people — you are not alone in it. You can act "as if" reality is right beside you — and start with something simple: touch, sound, smell. Small anchors like these don't argue with the feeling; they gently bring you back into contact with what is near.
unreality.practice: Touch something with a clear texture and name three sensations: temperature, weight, surface. Tell yourself "This is here" — and act "as if" reality were right beside you.

awe.text: The neo-romantic turn is what Vermeulen and van den Akker call the renewed interest in the sublime, in mystery, in a beauty larger than ourselves. The awe you felt is a precious feeling, and there's no need to cover it up with embarrassed irony. The Romantics sought to see the infinite in the everyday, and metamodernism once again allows us to do so without being embarrassed by our naivety. Your reverence is not sentimentality but openness to the fact that the world is bigger than any explanation. You can simply let yourself stand and look, without commenting. Metamodernism doesn't require you to explain this feeling, share it, or draw a conclusion from it: it is enough that it happened. Sometimes the best thing to do with awe is simply to stay quiet.
awe.practice: Stay with whatever filled you with awe for one more minute, without speaking and without taking a photo — no irony, no commentary. Notice what is happening in your body.

relief.text: A pendulum long held toward tension finally lets go — this is how metamodernism would see relief. This quiet and important feeling can be allowed to be here fully. Metamodernism describes life as oscillation, and relief is a natural part of that motion. After long tension, body and mind can finally straighten out a little. There's no need to devalue it with irony like "don't celebrate too soon" or "this won't last." The "New Sincerity" allows you to say to yourself plainly: I feel better, and that's good. You can simply enjoy this moment without hurrying on to the next worry. Relief reminds you that hard phases are not forever, and you can keep that knowledge for the future too.
relief.practice: Take a slow exhale and say to yourself plainly, without irony: "I feel lighter." Notice where in your body you feel it.

calm.text: Sitting, drinking tea, looking out the window — and not considering it banal: metamodernism gives simple states back their dignity. The calm you have right now doesn't need to be earned. Postmodern culture often suspected such states of being naive. Yet it is often in such minutes that what makes everything else worthwhile lives. The "New Sincerity" applies to calm too: you don't need to explain it, be ironic about it, or turn it into productivity. You can simply be in it while it lasts, without worrying that it will end: the pendulum will return to this place more than once. Calm doesn't have to be earned or useful — it is enough for it to be.
calm.practice: Sit for a minute, noticing one simple thing that is pleasant right now — warmth, light, quiet. Don't explain it or be ironic about it: simple things have their dignity back.

inspiration.text: "Pragmatic romanticism" is what Luke Turner's Metamodernist Manifesto calls the thing we can once again catch fire with. Inspiration is the joyful sense that something new has suddenly become possible. Vermeulen and van den Akker name enthusiasm as one of the poles between which the feeling of our time oscillates. After an era when enthusiasm seemed naive, you can once again catch fire in earnest. Inspiration is not a childish illusion but a chance to begin something, even knowing it won't all go perfectly. You can enjoy it now and take a first step while it's alive, without being ashamed of your passion. If the inspiration fades later, that too is part of the oscillation, not a sign that the idea was bad.
inspiration.practice: Write down the idea while it's fresh, in one or two sentences. Note one small step you could take as soon as tomorrow.

schadenfreude.text: Compilations of other people's failures, memes, mockery as a way of being "in the know" — the internet culture of recent decades is largely built on schadenfreude. So if you notice it in yourself, you are not alone, though it's awkward to admit. Postmodern irony made such mockery almost the norm. Metamodernism describes a turn in which this irony starts to feel cramped, and people once again dare to be sincere and compassionate — without giving up humor. There's no need to hide schadenfreude; it's worth acknowledging honestly. And then allowing yourself an "oscillation" — a swing toward the other pole: imagining what that person is going through right now. Laughter and compassion can exist side by side. You don't have to choose between them once and for all, but you can notice which way the pendulum is moving.
schadenfreude.practice: Admit to yourself: "Yes, I enjoyed that." Then ask: "And what is he or she feeling right now?" — and stay with the answer.

contempt.text: Someone who ridicules everything can never be caught being vulnerable — this is how Wallace, in "E Unibus Pluram," described irony and mocking superiority as self-protection. Contempt often works like the same armor: you look down on others, and nothing can touch you. Wallace also observed that over time this stance turns into a trap. Contempt is a relative of that irony: it lets you avoid feeling what lies beneath it — hurt, disappointment, fear. Metamodernism suggests not abandoning your critical eye, but swinging between it and sincere interest. The question "What did this person do to me?" is often more honest than "Why are they so pathetic?"
contempt.practice: In your mind, replace the phrase "They're pathetic" with "It hurt me that…" and finish it — silently or aloud.

disgust.text: "Cringe" — a burning embarrassment about your own sincerity, enthusiasm, things you once said — is practically the arch-enemy of the metamodern sensibility. Disgust, especially at yourself, can be very strong, and it is involuntary. Metamodern culture works with this cringe a great deal: in its films and books the characters are awkward, touching, "too much" — and that is exactly why they are alive. Their awkwardness turns out to be not a reason to look away but a chance to recognize yourself. Disgust at your own sincerity is an echo of the ironic era, when feeling in earnest was considered ridiculous. Metamodernism offers "informed naivety": knowing how you look from outside and still not turning away from yourself. Awkward doesn't mean unworthy. Often it is precisely in the awkward that the most alive part of us hides.
disgust.practice: Tell someone close one of your "cringe" moments and laugh about it together. Tell yourself: "It was awkward — and it was real."

revenge.text: Films and series where the wrongdoer gets what they deserve draw us in because they promise to restore justice — metamodernism suggests watching such plots "as if." The wish for revenge is born of hurt and injustice, and it is worth acknowledging honestly. Metamodernism describes the ability to live with big meanings "as if": to believe in a story while knowing it is a story. A revenge fantasy can be acknowledged as a fantasy — with all its force, but also with the understanding that life is more complicated than a script. "Informed naivety" here means honestly wanting justice while soberly remembering that revenge rarely brings the relief it promises. Beneath the fantasy there usually lies a simple need — for your pain to be acknowledged.
revenge.practice: Write down the revenge fantasy in full, like a scene from a film. Beneath it, one line: "What I really need is…".

anger_at_loved.text: "Default setting" is what Wallace, in "This Is Water," called the habit of seeing yourself as the center of the world — the habit that makes others look like obstacles in a queue or a traffic jam. Anger at the people close to you, which you feel ashamed of afterward, is a deeply human experience. Metamodernism describes the emotional life of our time as "oscillation" — a swinging between poles: hope and melancholy, enthusiasm and skepticism. Closeness also works like a pendulum: tenderness and irritation take turns, and one doesn't cancel the other. Wallace was talking about irritation with strangers, but the same happens with those we love. Stepping out of that setting doesn't mean not being angry; it means giving the other person back their depth. Anger doesn't give you the right to wound, but it doesn't make you a bad person either.
anger_at_loved.practice: When things are quieter, imagine this person's day through their eyes: what were they carrying today? Stay with that for a minute.

ambivalence.text: In Plato, Eros is a go-between, neither god nor mortal; from this "metaxy" Vermeulen and van den Akker derive the "meta" in metamodernism. Loving someone and not being able to stand them at the same time is hard, especially if it seems that feelings should be clear-cut. Metamodernism describes precisely a life "in between," where a person doesn't choose one pole but swings between them. For them this is an honest form of contemporary sensibility: you can be naive and knowing, hopeful and melancholic, all at once. Mixed feelings toward someone close are not a malfunction but the ordinary state of a living bond. You don't have to decide what you "really" feel. You can let the pendulum swing and notice which side outweighs the other at any given moment.
ambivalence.practice: Put one palm on your chest and the other on your belly: let one be "love," the other "can't stand." Breathe like this for a minute, choosing nothing.

guilty_relief.text: Laughing and crying, grieving and breathing out at the same time — metamodernism starts from the idea that contradictory feelings are not a mistake. Relief after a breakup, a parting, or even the death of a seriously ill loved one is often a source of shame, though it is very common. Relief does not cancel love. It speaks of the weight you were carrying — fear, caregiving, exhaustion. When that weight lifts, the body breathes out on its own, without asking permission. The metamodern "New Sincerity" suggests naming such a feeling plainly, without self-justification and without self-condemnation. You don't need to prove to yourself that you loved "correctly." You can simply acknowledge: I feel relief, and I loved. Love and relief are not competing with each other. Both sentences are true at once.
guilty_relief.practice: Say two sentences aloud, one after the other: "I feel relief" and "I loved / I love." Between them — not "but," only "and."

indifference.text: Between empathy and apathy — Vermeulen and van den Akker name this, too, among the poles of our time. Sometimes something "should" move you, and it doesn't, and that feels awkward. Indifference is not your final essence but one point on the pendulum's arc. Sometimes, after overload or long tension, it simply freezes at the pole of apathy. In "This Is Water," Wallace said that real freedom is the freedom to choose what you pay attention to. You can't choose a feeling, but you can choose your attention. There's no need to force yourself to empathize; you can only gently turn your gaze toward something and give a feeling the chance to come, if it wants to.
indifference.practice: Choose one small thing near you and look at it for a minute with full attention. Don't wait for a feeling — Wallace would say you can choose not the feeling but your attention.

escape.text: We know there is no perfect place, and we dream of it anyway — this is how Vermeulen and van den Akker describe the "neo-romanticism" of our time. The wish to drop everything and run away — from a job, a city, a role — says something important, and it is worth listening to. Metamodernism owes a great deal to German Romanticism, which called this longing for "somewhere out there" Sehnsucht — a yearning for the distant and the better. The dream of escape is neither naive nor foolish — it is a romantic desire that can be lived "as if": seriously imagining a different life while remembering that it too would be imperfect. Such a dream can tell you a lot about what is missing here. You don't need to decide anything big — it's enough to listen.
escape.practice: Describe in three sentences a day in the life you'd like to escape to. Note one detail you could add to today.

forbidden_attraction.text: Novalis's "blue flower" is a symbol of endless longing for what can never be fully attained. Attraction to someone unavailable, or the "wrong" person, can be confusing and frightening. Metamodernism takes a great deal from the Romantics, and the Romantics knew this feeling better than anyone. Vermeulen and van den Akker describe the metamodern sensibility as a striving for the unattainable that knows it is unattainable. Attraction to the unavailable often speaks of a longing for something bigger than the particular person: for a different life, for aliveness, for a different self. The attraction itself calls for neither condemnation nor action. You can approach it with "informed naivety": acknowledge its power and look with curiosity at what it's about.
forbidden_attraction.practice: Imagine that this attraction is your "blue flower": what exactly does it promise — what life, what version of you? Just look at the answer, deciding nothing.

social_anxiety.text: Television culture made us hyper-self-conscious, Wallace wrote in "E Unibus Pluram": we constantly see ourselves through the eyes of an imagined viewer. The fear of people and of being judged is agonizing: it seems everyone notices your every awkward moment. Social anxiety is largely an effect of this inner screen, not the truth about how others perceive you. Metamodernism offers "informed naivety": knowing that you may look awkward from outside — and still taking part, speaking, trying. It is precisely awkward sincerity, in Wallace's view, that makes a person alive. Others, most likely, are busy with their own inner screens too. To them you are as much a background as they are to you, and that is a little freeing.
social_anxiety.practice: Before a meeting, tell yourself: "I may look awkward — and still be here." Take one small step toward others.

uncertainty.text: Metamodernism moves forward even though it knows the truth may never be found — this thought from "Notes on Metamodernism" sounds almost like everyday advice. Uncertainty is hard: you want guarantees, and there aren't any. Metamodernism offers a particular stance for this. Drawing on Kant, Vermeulen and van den Akker speak of living "as if": acting as if the goal were achievable, even without being sure that it is. They call this stance "pragmatic idealism." Uncertainty requires neither blind faith nor despair. You can hold both doubt and hope in mind at the same time, and take the next step without knowing the whole road.
uncertainty.practice: Choose one small action for today and do it as if the road were already visible, even though you can see only the next step.

waiting.text: "Metaxy" — dwelling between two poles — is, for Vermeulen and van den Akker, the key to contemporary sensibility. Waiting — for an answer, for results, for news — leaves you suspended, where neither hope nor fear can win. Waiting is not empty time but a particular state in which the pendulum swings between "everything will be fine" and "everything is bad." Fighting this swinging is pointless; you can simply notice its rhythm, the way you notice your breathing. And allow yourself to live in the gaps: drink tea, talk to someone, look out the window. The pendulum's swinging doesn't cancel the fact that you are here. The answer will come in its own time, and these minutes are already your life.
waiting.practice: Set a timer for five minutes and do something simple with your hands. When it goes off, notice which way the pendulum has swung.

regret.text: The past as a game of quotations — that is often how postmodernism treated it; metamodernism once again takes its own history seriously. Regret over something done or left undone can hold on for a long time, and that is hard. Regret is worth living through sincerely, without hiding behind the irony of "oh well, whatever." But metamodernism also offers the other pole — sobriety: back then you knew less than you know now, and you acted within those circumstances. And the "as if" stance lets you look forward: act as if something could still be done differently — because often it really can. Swinging between pain about the past and hope for the future is not inconsistency but a living form of growing up.
regret.practice: Write: "I regret that…", and below it: "As if it were still possible, I could…". Notice what resonated.

longing.text: "I miss them" — without a smirk, without caveats: the metamodern "New Sincerity" gives such words their voice back. Longing for a particular person aches quietly and stubbornly. In an ironic culture such feelings were often hidden, as though longing were a little shameful. Vermeulen and van den Akker write that the metamodern sensibility oscillates between hope and melancholy. Longing, too, swings between these poles: at times you want them back, at times a gentle acceptance comes. You don't have to stop the pendulum. It swings because the bond was alive. Longing tells you that this person held a real place in your life, and acknowledging that is already a form of respect — for yourself and for them.
longing.practice: Write this person a letter you won't send. In it, simply say honestly what you miss.

world_pain.text: The financial crisis, ecological threats, the social upheavals of the new century — Vermeulen and van den Akker linked the emergence of the metamodern sensibility to this series of crises. Pain for the world — over wars, disasters, injustice — can be almost unbearable. At such a time irony stops saving us, and people once again want to believe the world can become better — while knowing how hard that is. They call this stance "pragmatic idealism." There's no need to be ashamed of your pain, and no need to drown in it. You can swing between grief and hope, allowing yourself both to weep for the world and to do something small in it. Hope here is not naivety but a decision to act "as if" change were possible.
world_pain.practice: Limit your time with the news and choose one small thing that will make the world a little gentler today — even if it's right next to you. This is pragmatic idealism on a small scale.

rejection.text: Irony long served as insurance: if you spoke about your feelings with a smirk, you couldn't truly be rejected. Rejection hurts, and it hurts especially if you opened up sincerely. Wallace suggested that the new rebels would be those who dared to speak in earnest, risking mockery and condescending smiles. Metamodernism describes this as the "New Sincerity" — a willingness to risk looking naive. Rejection is the price of sincerity, not proof that sincerity was a mistake. You did what many don't dare to do: you opened up without armor. It hurts, but it also speaks of your courage. The refusal belongs to this one encounter, not to your right to feel.
rejection.practice: Sit or stand up straight, put a hand on your chest and say aloud: "I took a risk and opened up." Say it as an acknowledgment of courage, not of a mistake.

abandonment.text: Instability and the sense that anything can change at any moment — this, in large part, is the "structure of feeling" of our era. The fear of being abandoned can sit deep and surface even on calm days, and there is nothing shameful in it. Your fear is not only a personal story but also a response to that shared climate. And the metamodern "as if" stance offers a gentle way of living with it: trusting "as if" the bond is reliable, without demanding absolute guarantees from it. This is not naivety but "informed naivety": you know the risks — and you still choose trust. Trust here is not carelessness but a courage you choose again.
abandonment.practice: Recall a time when someone stayed by your side even though they could have left, and stay inside that memory for a minute. Return to it when the fear comes back.

unrequited.text: Trying in spite of inevitable failure and seeking what you may never find — this formula of Vermeulen and van den Akker sounds almost like a description of unrequited love. When you love without being loved back, the strength of the feeling meets its impossibility, and that is exhausting. There is nothing foolish in your feeling: it is one of the most romantic, most "metamodern" forms of sincerity — to love in earnest without guarantees. But metamodernism is also oscillation: beside the pole of hope there is the pole of sobriety. You can respect your feeling and at the same time, gradually, let it grow quieter. Love without return does not diminish your capacity to love. That capacity is simply looking for another place to go.
unrequited.practice: Today, do one thing that belongs only to you — a favourite walk, a dish, a song. Respect your feeling and let it rest a little.

humiliation.text: Yawns, rolled eyes, cool smiles, cries of "Oh how banal" — in "E Unibus Pluram," Wallace warned that the new rebels would have to withstand all of this. When someone tries to make you look ridiculous or worthless, it wounds deeply, and you have a right to this pain. Ironic culture turned mockery into a weapon: to ridicule is to be above. Wallace saw the willingness to withstand mockery not as a disgrace but as courage. If we continue Wallace's thought, humiliation says more about those who use mockery as armor than about you. Your sincerity, your feelings and your dignity are not made smaller because someone laughed at them. Sometimes what gets ridiculed turns out to be the most alive.
humiliation.practice: Write down what about you someone tried to ridicule. Below it, write why it is valuable to you.

body_shame.text: A culture of surfaces and images, where everything turns into a picture — that is how postmodernity is often described, and the social media feed is its direct heir. If you dislike your body right now, that is very common, and there's nothing to be ashamed of in it. Metamodernism describes a desire to bring back depth — what lies behind the picture. Your body is not an image but the place where you live, feel, embrace, get tired. "Informed naivety" lets you know about beauty standards and still treat your body with sincere warmth — not because it measures up, but because it is yours. You can swing between criticism and tenderness, but give tenderness a little more room.
body_shame.practice: Name one part of your body and one thing it does for you. Say "thank you" to it — in earnest, without irony.

illness.text: Even amid tedious, difficult everyday life you can choose what to pay attention to — Wallace said so in "This Is Water." When your body lets you down and takes away your strength and your familiar rhythm, it is hard, and you have every right to be sad and angry. Metamodernism speaks of oscillation between hope and melancholy, and in illness this pendulum is especially noticeable: today it seems everything will be all right, tomorrow that there's no strength left. This swinging is natural and doesn't need fixing. That doesn't cancel the pain or require you to be cheerful. But sometimes attention to something small — a warm cup, light, the voice of someone close — gives you something to hold on to when the bigger supports are temporarily out of reach.
illness.practice: Find one small pleasant thing in this day — a taste, a sound, some light — and, as Wallace advised, choose to look at it. Let your attention rest on it for a minute.

pride.text: "Oh, it's nothing" — this is how ironic culture taught us to play down our achievements, so as not to seem immodest. Pride in something you've done is a good, well-earned feeling. The metamodern "New Sincerity" gives back the right to rejoice in your work openly. Telling yourself "I did this, and it's good" is not bragging but honesty. At the same time, metamodernism keeps the oscillation: you can be proud while also remembering the doubts, the difficulties, the help of others. Such pride is not arrogant and belittles no one: it is warm, rather like gratitude to yourself for persevering. Let yourself enjoy it without rushing to add "oh, it's nothing." Pride lived in earnest makes you more generous toward others too.
pride.practice: Say aloud: "I did this." Don't add irony or caveats — just stay with those words for a moment.

melancholy.text: Sad, but warm — many metamodern films and songs live in this tone, and Vermeulen and van den Akker describe our era as an oscillation between hope and melancholy. The gentle sadness you feel is one of the most metamodern of feelings. Metamodernism is heir to the Romantics, for whom melancholy was not an illness but a sensitivity to the infinite showing through the everyday. Novalis called on us to "romanticize" the world — to give the familiar a sense of mystery. Such sadness is a way of seeing the world more deeply: noticing that everything passes, and so becomes more precious. You don't need to climb out of it; you can savor it, like good music at dusk. Dusk, an old song, an empty street after rain — such things make this tone audible.
melancholy.practice: Step outside at dusk or go to a window and watch the light change for a minute — "romanticizing" the familiar view, as Novalis advised.
